units.title: First Steps & Introductions
units.description: Greetings, introducing yourself, polite everyday phrases, and foundational pronunciation rules.

lessons.title: Greetings & Politeness
lessons.summary: Master formal (Sie) vs. informal (du) greetings across Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

exercises.prompt: How do you formally say 'Good morning' in German?
exercises.explanation: 'Guten Morgen' is used until roughly 11:00 AM. In formal situations, you can pair it with 'Herr' (Mr.) or 'Frau' (Ms.).
exercises.grammar_tip: Time greetings take the accusative case masculine ending (-en): Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend.

exercises.prompt: Translate 'Nice to meet you (pleased to meet you)':
exercises.explanation: 'Freut mich' is a natural short form of 'Es freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen' (It pleases me to get to know you).

exercises.prompt: Match the German greeting with its English meaning:
exercises.explanation: 'Auf Wiedersehen' translates literally to 'until we see each other again'. On the phone, Germans say 'Auf Wiederhören'.
exercises.grammar_tip: 'Ihnen' is the capitalized dative formal pronoun for 'you'.

flashcards.grammar_note: Accusative masculine form (der Tag -> guten Tag).

flashcards.example_de: Auf Wiedersehen und einen schönen Tag noch!
flashcards.example_en: Goodbye and have a nice day!
flashcards.grammar_note: Standard polite closing phrase across the DACH region.

flashcards.example_en: Thank you very much for your help.
flashcards.grammar_note: The polite answer is 'Bitte schön' (You are welcome).

lessons.title: Articles & The Gender Matrix (Der, Die, Das)
lessons.summary: Understand how German assigns masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das) genders to every noun.

exercises.prompt: Select the correct article for: 'Bahnhof' (train station)
exercises.explanation: 'Bahnhof' is masculine (der Bahnhof). Compound nouns take the gender of the last word: der Hof -> der Bahnhof.
exercises.grammar_tip: Rule: All compound nouns take the gender of their final noun component.

exercises.explanation: 'Straße' is feminine (die Straße). Over 90% of nouns ending in '-e' denoting inanimate things are feminine.
exercises.grammar_tip: Rule: Nouns ending in -e are almost always feminine (die).

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct neuter article: '___ Rathaus steht am Marktplatz.'
exercises.explanation: 'Rathaus' (town hall) is neuter because 'das Haus' is neuter: das Rat + Haus = das Rathaus.
exercises.grammar_tip: Neuter nouns often end in -ment, -um, -chen, or -lein.

flashcards.example_de: Der Zug fährt pünktlich am Bahnhof ab.
flashcards.example_en: The train departs on time from the train station.
flashcards.grammar_note: Masculine noun (der). Plural forms with an Umlaut (ä).

flashcards.example_de: Die Straße ist ruhig und sauber.
flashcards.example_en: The street is quiet and clean.
flashcards.grammar_note: Feminine noun (die). Notice the 'ß' (Eszett) following a long vowel.

flashcards.example_de: Das historische Rathaus befindet sich im Zentrum.
flashcards.example_en: The historical town hall is located in the city center.
flashcards.grammar_note: Neuter noun (das). Compound noun ending in 'das Haus'.

questions.prompt: Welcher Artikel ist richtig? '___ Apfel ist rot.' (The apple is red)
questions.explanation: 'Apfel' is masculine in German: der Apfel.

questions.prompt: Was bedeutet 'Ich hätte gerne ein Wasser, bitte'?
options: I would like a water, please
questions.correct_answer: I would like a water, please
questions.explanation: 'Ich hätte gerne...' is the polite Konjunktiv II form for ordering food and drinks.

questions.prompt: Welche Verbform passt? 'Wir ___ aus Deutschland.' (We come from Germany)
questions.explanation: The 1st person plural subject 'wir' takes the '-en' ending: wir kommen.
